answers.text: Use a fixed three-line template — drop-off time, pallet count, damage — always in that order. Define each line exactly — time only, pallet count alone, damage or 'none' — no overlap between lines. If any field is missing, say to write 'not stated', never leave it blank or invent a figure.

Specify the list structure exactly: one line per call, fixed fields, a follow-up flag on each. State that the follow-up count is derived by summing the flagged entries, not asserted separately. Say explicitly what to do with a duplicate-looking entry — flag it, don't silently merge or drop it.
The timing in this note doesn't reconcile with itself. The six-hour estimate from an 8am start resolves same-day, so the note's finish date doesn't follow.
The growth figure doesn't hold up: 118 against 96 is roughly 23%, not 20%. Run separately, 9 out of 118 late gives about 92% on-time — that figure holds up.
Output 2 is the one to approve, since the number is derived, not asserted. What's missing from Output 1 is the 940 and the 827 themselves.
Email 2 is the one to send unchanged, since the volume increase is traceable to the PO log. The claim in Email 1 that can't be checked is the rate expectation itself; nothing supports it.

I'd treat the rates and retainer cap as sensitive by default — redact or confirm the tool's vetted first. The non-disclosure clause names both parties directly, its own reason for caution beyond the rates. The general scope of service carries little risk and can go in unredacted.
The check is a fixed cross-cast — recalculate from the warehouse system, set against the drafted summary. That check sits right before the reconciliation reaches finance, not earlier in the process.
Step 1 — extracting line items and totals — carries risk that compounds through every step after. Step 4 is where an error becomes irreversible — once it auto-submits, there's no catching it after.
